# Executive summary 

A particularly quiet quarter for consumption against a backdrop of macro economic uncertainty and no clear direction emerging from the USA, Europe or China has led us to revise our estimates lower for 2012, with a particular focus on consumption.  The production outlook has not deteriorated to the same extent, despite ongoing disruptions, and we are now forecasting a market in balance this year.  A meagre surplus of ~43kt pushes stocks out to 52 days of consumption for 2012 compared to 48 days in our previous LTO.  Our average price for this year is now slightly lower at $7997/t ($3.63/lb) down from $8048/t ($3.65/lb) in 2012$.  This reflects the weaker trend in copper prices over the April to August period in particular.  We remain of the view that prices will trade higher over the final quarter of this year as sentiment improves and government measures instil some confidence and encourage shoots of economic recovery. 

Based on a thorough review of market trends through the first half of 2012 and into the third quarter of the year we have downgraded our projection of world refined consumption growth to 1.9% from 2.7% in our last Long Term Outlook.  The main region where we have felt compelled to cut our full year 2012 forecast is Europe, particularly Western Europe.  The contagion from the political stalemate and policy stagnation over the Eurozone crisis has now spilled over into the copper products and wire and cable market to a much larger extent than had been feared.  With no imminent resolution in sight we feel it is only prudent to downgrade our expectations for the balance of the year.  We have therefore revised down our view on Europe as a whole to a 7.1% decline.  Germany, as the largest refined consumer and exporter of copper products, has unavoidably been hit by the slowdown in the rest of Europe, even though its own usage has been relatively robust, driven by the automotive industry.  Our projections for Chinese growth have also been scaled back slightly to 6.25% from 7%. 

Overall base case production capability is forecast to rise from 16.2Mt in 2011 to 21.1Mt by 2015, an increase of 30%. Beyond 2015 mine production is forecast to decline due to reserve depletion to reach 15.7Mt by 2025.  This means that over the forecast period, base case production capability will fall at an average rate of 0.2% p.a.  In 2011, demand for mine production exceeded available base case supply by c.375kt, lower than our Q2 estimate of around 430kt but within the range of analysis over the course of this year.  We expect the market to be effectively balanced this year with prim

ary supply exceeding demand by just 55kt, while metal from base case mines under construction and those projects currently in our ‘highly probable’ category will push the market into surplus from 2013 to 2016.  From 2016 onwards, demand for mine output should once again exceed available base case plus highly probable supply. 

Our smelter production capability forecast for 2012 is 16.3Mt, representing a 5.9% increase from 2011, although lack of concentrates and scrap is likely to moderate this increase to just 3.0% in terms of actual production.  Smelter output capability growth is expected to remain strong over the next two years at 10.0% in 2013 and 6.7% in 2014, primarily as a result of increased mine feed although increasing smelter capacity in China and India should also contribute.  A total of 5.1Mt of additional smelter production capability is expected over the forecast period with over half coming from China. 

The majority of the revisions made to our smelter production capability forecasts are largely reflected in the changes to our refinery output estimates and these can be seen in the main chapter.  Taking these into account, base case global copper refined production reached 19.7Mt/a in 2011 (+3.6%), while capability is expected to increase by a substantial 6.9% this year, to 21.0Mt.  A further 11% year-on-year increment in 2013 will see this figure rise to 23.3Mt/a in 2013, and then to 25.2Mt in 2014.  However, growth is forecast to slow in 2015, and then to decline from 2016 onwards.  As a consequence, overall global capability will increase by only 1.6% p.a. between 2010 and 2025.  In tonnage terms this equates to an increase of ~4.74Mt to 23.38Mt in 2025. 

It will take some time for the new supply that we forecast to refill the stock pipeline.  As surpluses slowly emerge and stocks are replenished and build towards the long-term average of 65 days of consumption, we expect prices to ease back in 2014 to average $7125/t ($3.05/lb) in constant 2012$ terms.  Beyond 2015 as production continues to come through and bulging surpluses push inventories of metal to over 80 days of consumption by 2016 we anticipate that prices will retreat sharply to reach lows of around $5512/t ($2.50/lb) in 2012$ on average in both 2017 and 2018.  These lower prices will constrain scrap availability and we expect consumers will become slightly more heavily reliant on refined metal over that period.  In addition, the lower prices will likely lead to cutbacks in production of high cost producers (particularly in China where mine output is very price sensitive).  We would also anticipate some projects will be deferred, delayed or ramped up at a slower pace than planned. 

<mark>Beyond 2018 and through to 2025 we expect prices to average at our project incentive price of $6614/t ($3.00/lb) in constant 2012$.  These forecasts remain well above the 90th percentile of C1 cash costs on a Composite Costing basis. Historically, marginal costs have been a good pr

oxy for determining where annual average copper prices will decline to, but only during periods of excessive metal inventories. However, our analysis points to only moderate metal surpluses occurring at certain stages over the forecast period, reflecting a market that continues to struggle to keep up with consumption and maintain stocks at the average 65 days of consumption over the medium to long term. ## China 

**Disappointing third quarter leads to downgrade in 2012 annual growth** The third quarter of 2012 failed to deliver the first tangible signs of an accelerating upturn in semi manufactures production that had been expected.  From recent evidence it is now clear that the degree of inventory overhang through the supply chain is more extensive than had been thought.  As a result, the mild increase in wire and cable orders from final consumers has been met by the drawing down of existing stocks of wire rod without the need to immediately replenish them with new orders from the rod industry.  Wire and cable manufacturers encouragingly reported an increase in their capacity utilisation rates during August, along with a sharp drop in their raw material inventories, in response to the placing of new copper power cable orders by the State Power Grids and a modest increase in building wire demand.  Unfortunately, the initial influx of these orders has not been of the magnitude that was expected due to some delays in the tendering process.   However, the sentiment of the wire and cable sector has changed for the better with the number of companies surveyed now expecting to see improved order books over the remaining balance of the year.  A decisive turning point appears to have been reached and a steady inflow of new power cable orders, the largest volume product line in the Chinese consumption matrix, will inevitably result in the belated upturn in rod production in the fourth quarter.  However because of the stagnant third quarter our forecast of a 7.0% increase in refined consumption in 2012 is now unlikely to be met.  We have therefore revised down our projection of growth this year to 6.25%. 

**Stimulus measures are an encouraging early signal** The stimulus measures announced in early-September are a promising indicator for future demand signifying that Chinese policymakers have realised that they must intervene to stimulate growth now that the battle over inflation has largely been won.  The measures include 25 subway and intercity railway projects for 18 cities.  Railway spending plans have been revised up three times since July to 496Bn yuan and are clearly a centre piece of Premier Wen Jiaboa’s plans to stabilise economic expansion by promoting investment.  The railway and subway investments will boost consumption of copper in trackside cables, overhead electrification conductors and in locomotive engines.  Although copper use in railway infrastructure probably amounts to no more than 2% of Chinese total consumption, and the other sectors targeted by the stimulus such as road building, waterway, sewage treatment plants and port and warehouse projects are even les

s copper intensive, it is the increasing likelihood that further measures will be forthcoming that has boosted sentiment. The China Electricity Council announced that total power consumption rose by 5.5% in the first six months of 2012 with growth dragged down by lower power use by Metals Market Service Long Term Outlook - September 2012 Page 5 of 37 Copper Long Term Outlook industrial and high energy consuming sectors. However year-on-year growth in the second half of 2012 would accelerate to between 6-8%. This would take total electricity use in 2012 up to 6-7%. Electricity consumption, a key barometer of industrial economic activity and copper consumption, would therefore see an acceleration in growth in the second half of 2012 compared to the first half. Plans to increase house building by 86M units are also favourable. **Home appliance sector is still struggling, unlike automotive** The one main area of Chinese copper consumption that is clearly still very weak are home appliances. Facing unexpectedly weak overseas demand, stocks of finished goods have built up at factories and warehouses and distributors. This has forced home appliance manufacturers to take extended shutdowns over the summer to help the backlog to clear. In some segments inventories have moderated back to more normal levels but there is yet to be either an internal or external boost to demand to rekindle an expansion in home appliance production. The most revealing indicators for Jan-Aug 2012 are a modest 1.9% year-on-year increase in air conditioner output, a 0.5% contraction in refrigerator production and a 5.8% slump in AC motor shipments, the key barometer for the large volume Chinese winding wire business. In the past, increasing shipments to overseas markets was the main mechanism to counteract domestic inventory accumulations, but this option is not available in dismal home appliance markets globally. Compared to the situation in the appliance sector, the automotive sector is in much better shape. But whereas the automotive industry endured a tough 2011, the appliance industry had a bumper year, so perhaps the baton can be passed to the appliance industry in 2013. Automobile production rose 8.2% year-on-year in the Jan-Aug period of 2012 and export sales of automobile components increased at a 13.5% rate to serve the still buoyant automobile sector around the world. ##### **Chinese production of copper and copper alloy products - (kt)** 40 3500

**Semis industry still planning and commissioning new capacity aggressively** Despite the temporarily weaker and slower development of the market, existin

g and new players are committing heavily to building and commissioning new semis capacity.  The bulk of these new projects are concentrated on copper wire rod plants which are viewed as the most attractive and least riskiest investments.  The mills can be constructed and commissioned in a relatively short period of time (12-18 months) and can be ramped up fairly quickly once production has commenced to make a uniform commodity product.  Moreover, the rod is targeted to serve the large volume copper power cable and winding wire markets so there are many potential customers available.  The present scale of capacity commissioning is considerably in excess of likely market growth and the potential to replace imports from overseas but this has not hindered the tempo or number of projects.  Over 2.5Mt of new rod capacity was opened in 2011 and a further 3.9Mt is scheduled for the 2012-14 period.  Much new capacity has been commissioned in the plate, sheet and strip sector in the past year but operators have been struggling to raise capacity utilisation much above 50% due to weak short term market conditions and the technical difficulties of casting and rolling complex alloys.   Ample capacity is already in place in the copper tube and pipe sector to meet projected requirements in the medium term and only small scale projects are being attempted. 

**The potential for future copper consumption growth is undiminished** In ferrous markets there has been much debate over whether there has been a structural shift in China towards a permanently lower level of growth as the peak of steel demand intensity may be past.  In copper we are confident that although the annual growth rate is reduced due to the base effect the potential contribution from additional tonnage is undiminished.  Aside from population growth, the most important long term drivers of copper usage will be electricity demand, urbanisation and rising per capita income levels.   Moreover as China transitions towards becoming a net exporter of copper semi-manufactures as well as wire and cable and finished products (as it is already) its copper intensity will continue to rise as it steadily replaces the volumes of semis imports by its own production and exports more to nearby overseas markets.  This element of growth is a positive structural change that is largely independent of China’s own economic development.   It is instead a function

The market has been tracking last year’s levels for much of this year, but month to month variations have been erratic with a strong performance in one month often giving way to a weaker showing in the following month. Wire rod has exhibited the marginally stronger trend with production flat in H1 2012, although output in both May and June was slightly above the year-ago comparisons. This has left comparatively less scope for US wire and cable manufacturers to increase their own production. The domestic market is anxiously awaiting a revival from the ailing construction sector. **Start up of SDI La Farga marks structural change** The start up of the SDI La Farga rod mill in New Haven, Indiana, would appear to mark the beginnings a structural change in North American consumption. Direct scrap use in wire rod production has typically never been more than 1-1.5% of the regional total and has always been restricted to a small proportion of high grade No.1 scrap as top up feed. The new mill is modelled upon the technology in use at La Farga Group’s facility north of Barcelona in Spain which makes rod utilising No.2 smelter grade scrap. The quality of rod produced is suitable for the vast majority of applications, except for very sophisticated applications or where the wire is drawn to a very fine diameter prior to use. The mill is currently in trial operation but has yet to begin

commercial production. The success of the operation will be governed by the acceptance and testing of trial batches of rod by wire and cable manufacturers. If the mill is a commercial success then it will increase direct scrap use at the expense of either US refined consumption or rod imports from Canada. Greater direct scrap use in the US will restrict scrap exports to China, tightening scrap availability there for smelters who supplement their concentrate feed. Demand seemed to shrug off the negative backdrop in the first quarter, with activity turning higher from Q4 2011, although restocking was at least partly responsible for the upturn. Since then, consumption has been increasingly sluggish with the result that summer shutdowns at semis producers were longer than usual in August. Only the comparis

on with a particularly weak fourth quarter last year will prevent Western Europe from a seventh consecutive year-on-year contraction in the final three months of 2012. 

**Present weakness illustrates future trends** The current weakness of demand brings the longer term prospects for Western Europe sharply into focus.  Consumption in the region peaked at just over 4Mt back in 2000 and its downward path has been barely interrupted since then to the point that our latest forecast for refined consumption this year is even lower than the financial crisis nadir of 2009.  During this period there has been rationalisation of both first and end users of copper, which fits neatly with our own long term projections of declining first use demand out to 2025.  This clearly points to further rationalisation and thus the closure of some semis capacity in the region.  However, just as there will be losers in the traditional consumers in the west of the region, there will be winners elsewhere, with gains to be centred in Eastern Europe and Poland and Russia in particular. 

**Germany bears the brunt of regional downgrade** The downgrade to our estimate of 2012 refined demand in Europe is concentrated in the west, with the 92kt cut to German prospects taking the brunt of the 166kt which has been slashed from the region as a whole.  We have also revised down expectations for most of the rest, although Poland stands out as the only major regional player to enjoy an upgrade after a promising first half.  As a result of these changes we now expect total European demand to decline by 7.1% this year to 3.723Mt.  We do, however, expect a better percentage growth outturn in 2013 than previously and now forecast a c.4% expansion over 2013 and 2014.  From then on the negative headwinds for the region as a whole lead to consumption slowing and then moving into decline in the latter part of our forecast period.

**Digging to basement levels** The demand picture in Europe is not simply a question of an East to West divide but there is also a North to South split in terms of which markets are performing best, with the end use segment that most clearly illustrates this trend being construction.  Even putting the most positive spin on the overall construction market would describe it as sluggish but the picture for Southern Europe is much worse.  Total construction investment in the Eurozone has been contracting since 2008 but it is particularly worrying that this trend is far from over.  In fact, investment is not forecast to return to 2011 levels until 2018.  Investment in 2011 was itself down some 16% from the 2007 peak.  Over the same period investment in construction in Italy is down 18%, while in Spain it has contracted by a whopping 34%.  These historic trends have not changed course either, with market participants reporting that building wire demand remains weakest in

the south of the region but better in the countries of Northern Europe.  At some point there will be a bounce back but according to our forecasts this will not be in the short or medium term. 

**Automotive forecasts indicate east** The strength in end use demand from the automotive market so far this year has been less to do with production levels and more do to with the types of vehicles that have been produced.  Total European vehicle production is estimated to fall by around 2% to 20.8m vehicles in 2008 but despite this automotive has been one of the few bright spots for demand.  This has been because of reasonable production of highly copper intensive German high end vehicles in addition to solid exports of automotive components such as wiring harnesses. However, we are now hearing that even this market has slowed somewhat as exports of cars to Asian countries, China in particular, are now slowing.  The good news though is that after a downturn in motor vehicle production this year, next year is forecast to recover and expand at c. 4% through 2013 to 2014.  Beyond that, regional growth is expected to be muted, with this largely focussed on Eastern European countries as traditional producers in the west of the region gradually shift their production to lower cost locations.  OEMs will also follow this trend, with the result being a sectoral demand profile very similar to overall regional consumption growth. 

**No spark of life for electric infrastructure** The near term demand prospects for the electrical sector have also faced some negative headwinds of late, amid German caution over infrastructure investment to support the development of offshore wind farms.  As we noted in our Insight _Blowin’ in the wind_ , although wind turbines do consume significant quantities of copper, this can be dwarfed by the requirement for infrastructure to support them, particularly when wind farms are offshore.  However, despite this near term set back, the longer term outlook remains reasonable for the sector as a result of the requirement for investment in new sources of power in Germany and across Europe.  The European Union has mandated that by 2020 20% of energy should be generated from renewable sources.  Whichever options countries choose for meeting this, inevitably this will lead to further localisation and investment in the grid.  This will underpin sectoral demand for copper through the forecast period.

Overseas markets would likely be weak in any case but the attractiveness of the Yen as a safe haven currency, and its resulting appreciation against a basket of currencies, cannot be helping Japanese firms sell their goods abroad. Economic theory would suggest that currency strength would not make much difference to buying patterns in the short term but over the longer term consumers would look for cheaper alternatives. At the same time Japanese manufacturers of finished goods are also looking to maintain their own competitiveness. Famed for excellence and efficiency in manufacturing processes there surely comes a tipping point when there are few savings left to be made. ## Asia (excluding China and Japan) **South Korea is now struggling in China’s lengthening shadow** The stimulus measures that kick-started the domestic Chinese economy in the wake of the global financial crisis in 2009/10 provided the last big shot of adrenaline into South Korea’s export focussed economy. Domestic copper consumption benefitted from the sharp initial surge in copper rod and wire exports in 2009, followed by a later surge in brass mill exports in 2010, but since then the tide has turned as the growing volume and quality of China’s own production has replaced the need for imports from South Korea. Korea’s exports of rod and drawn wire have plunged from 167kt in 2009 to a projected total of only 60kt for 2012 and this, to an overwhelming degree, explains the slump in the country’s refined copper consumption since 2010. Exports of brass mill products have held up rather better as local fabricators have been more able to differentiate their superior quality and characteristics in these product lines than in commodity rod and wire products. This is the key challenge that Korean semi manufacturers face in the next decade. Semis exports are now in long term decline while South Korea is a logical nearby target for fledgling Chinese semis exporters to sell to over the next few years. **But power shortage needs a solution** Faced with a challenging external sector, South Korea’s prospects now depend more than ever on the outlook for domestic use, and here there are some opportunities. The country’s per capita consumption is already quite high, at 16.5kg per person in 2011, and this is for two main reasons. Firstly the nation is a major exporter of copper semis, wire and cable and other copper containing intermediate and final goods (such as cars and consumer electronics) and secondly it is a large consumer of energy which also stimulates copper use. South Korea is capable of generating 76M kilowatts of electricity, but its use is close to this level and a power black out is a real threat. Nearly 50M kilowatts are consumed by the country’s factories and assembly lines that run all year long. Meanwhile the 26M kilowatts of consumer use is stretched by the extreme climate which demands constant heating in the winter and cooling in the summer. The ever expanding requirement for power will require a further 14 nuclear power plants by 2024 and this will necessitate a strengthening and reinforcement of the national transmission and distribution network that will be favourable for domestic wire and cable consumption, as are market conditions currently. T

he other main opportunity is in the country’s downstream exports of wire and cable and intermediate and final goods. South Korea remains a price competitive exporter with superior product quality. The ASEAN Free Trade Area was formed in 1992 with the objective of increasing the region’s competiveness through the elimination of tariff and non-tariff barriers within the zone and to encourage investment into the area. Beyond 2015 mine production is forecast to decline due to reserve depletion to reach 15.7Mt by 2025. In 2011, demand for mine production exceeded available base case supply by c.375kt, lower than our Q2 estimate of around 430kt but within the range of analysis over the course of this year.  We expect the market to be effectively balanced this year with primary supply exceeding demand by just 55kt, while metal from base case mines under construction and those projects currently in our ‘highly probable’ category will push the market into surplus from 2013 to 2016. 

From 2016 onwards, demand for mine output should once again exceed available base case plus highly probable supply.  This shortfall will be satisfied either by the reactivation of closed mines, new ore discoveries at currently producing mines, incremental expansions, mine life extensions or the development of greenfield projects.  Highly probable, probable and possible projects have been selected based upon various criteria, including stage of advancement, potential project returns, technical impediments, country risk, company strategy and the ability of the owner to raise finance. 

There are clearly uncertainties associated with the judgement of impediments, country risk, company strategy and the ability of the owner, as to which of these projects should be included and, equally critically, when first commercial production might be expected.  While we assume that 100% of the projects listed in our highly probable category will be commissioned, history has shown that a good proxy to other project development can be derived by allocating ~70% of production from brownfield (inclusive of probable identified restarts and extensions) probable projects and 50% of from greenfield probable projects. l make up of projects developed will be a combination of these aforementioned categories plus so-called currently ‘off-radar’ projects and from a small proportion of projects in our possible category. # Trends in consumption of secondary copper 

## Scrap definition 

Copper scrap is classified into two general categories called old and new scrap.  New scrap, or manufacturing scrap, is generated during the fabrication of copper products and returned to the mill for reprocessing, or sold, and is not considered a new source of copper supply.  A manufacturer may generate up to 60% of scrap as clippings, trimmings, stampings, borings, and turnings when processing copper and copper-based products into finished articles.  New scrap is termed "run-around" or home scrap (which does not enter the scrap statistics) when it is generated internally at the plant re-using it, or it may be called "purchased return scrap" when returned by a customer from a plant external to that purchasing and re-using it.  Old scrap is generated from worn out, discarded or obsolete copper products and thus, is considered to be a “new” source of supply. 

## Scrapping rates 

The availability of _old_ copper scrap is linked to the volume of copper-containing products installed/purchased and their life cycles, or duration.  The life of copper in electrical equipment and machinery averages 30-35 years; in non-electrical machinery, 15 years; in housing, 35-75 years; in transportation, 10 years; and in all other sectors, about 10 years.  The average for the industry is estimated to be 15-20 years.  The rate of (old) scrap recovery and its availability to the market is limited not only by copper's long life, but also by the sensitivity of scrap collection rates to market prices. 

Over the past 20 years, the volume of _new_ copper scrap has not grown in line with industrial consumption of copper because manufacturing efficiencies have improved, leading to as much as a 50% fall in new scrap generation over the period. 

## Scrap usage 

Most old scrap recovered from the market place must be reprocessed either by smelting and refining, or, to a lesser extent, by leaching and electrowinning to form a pure copper product.  Fire refining in a reverberatory or other furnace may be sufficient for the better grades of scrap.  This latter process uses oxidation, fluxing and reduction, with a refined ingot, wire bar, slab, or billet usually being the end product. 

Certain products, such as brass rod (manufactured using 90-95% scrap) can contain higher amounts of scrap than others while still maintaining product quality tolerance.  Others, such as wire rod, must contain far less impurities (typically 5%) since these could affect the drawability (leading to snapping) of the wire rod in producing wire.  New scrap is readily used by brass and copper tube mills to generate new semi-fabricated forms with little additional treatment. Because minimal clean-up procedures are needed, this type of scrap is commonly called "direct melt", or No.1 scrap.  In general, No. 1 scrap is contained in copper and copper-alloy products,

rather than wire rod.  Scrap purchases by brass mills are based primarily on activity levels at the mills and the relative price differential between cathode and No. 1 scrap, rather than the actual copper price.  When business conditions are strong, brass mills have access to large volumes of return scrap.  When manufacturing (and, possibly imports) decline, mills may be forced to increase their cathode purchases. 

Low copper prices over the period 1997-2003 led to a reduction in the availability of smelting and refining grade scrap with a corresponding decline in the processing of this material in countries such the USA and in Europe.  The notable exception has been China where there has been an upward trend in the treatment of smelting and refining grade scrap material.  Economic and environmental considerations have also played a major role, with the cost of environmental compliance often leading to plant closures, particularly in the USA.  This is despite the fact that the cost of recovering one tonne of copper from scrap is approximately half that of recovery through the conventional route (concentratesmelting-refining).  Secondary smelters and ingot markers typically consume the lion's share (90%) of No.2 scrap and most of the auto radiators and red brass scrap. 

## Scrap consumption 

Copper produced from scrap (at smelters, refineries and in direct use) amounted to 8.33Mt in 2011, an increase of 4.6% on the prior year and accounting for 34% of copper consumed.  Direct use scrap took the lions share, representing some 57% of copper produced from scrap, with smelters (27%) and refineries (16%) producing copper from the balance. 

Growth in scrap use slowed in 2011 following the strong recovery in 2010, as a slowdown in the rate of price increase resulted slowed the relative increase in incentive to collect scrap while sluggish industrial production also limited scrap generation. # Principal uses of copper 

Copper consumption can be divided into three main product groups which are copper wire rod, copper products and copper alloy products.  Copper wire rod, which accounts for an estimated 55% of total Global consumption (i.e. including scrap) and ~70% of primary consumption, is copper’s main first use.  With the exception of silver, copper has the highest electrical conductivity of all the metals.  This helps to explain why the principal application for copper wire rod is wire and cable.  Wire rod is consumed in five main wire and cable markets which include general and industrial cable, utility power cable, telecommunication cable, other insulated wire and winding wire. 

In general, wire and cable and copper products are consumed in five broad sectors: construction, electric and electronic products, industrial machinery and equipment, transportation equipment and consumer and general products.  Of these, construction is one of the largest sectors for consuming copper, accounting for 31% of total copper consumption.  The main wire and cable and copper products consumed in the construction industry include building wire, power cable, copper plumbing and air conditioning tube, copper sheet and alloy products. 

Building wire is the largest of the wire and cable markets, accounting for ~35% of wire rod consumption.  Rising intensity of use, in both the mature and developing economies, will be largely responsible for building wire maintaining this position.  The number of electrical appliances used at home and at the workplace continues to rise, particularly in the mature economies, thereby leading to an increase in the number of power outlets needed per building.  In addition, recent technical issues imply that more copper wire and cable will be needed in the future.  One of these issues, electrical energy efficiency involves using less power to perform a given task by using more or heavier copper conductors.  Finally, good power quality, defined as the uninterrupted, undistorted flow of electricity at the correct voltage, is also helping to drive up the demand for building wire due to higher power quality being achieved by installing additional circuits and heavier wires and cables. 

In cont

rast to the building and industrial cable market, the power utility market is the smallest of all the wire and cable segments.  However, demand growth for power cable will be supported by both the general recovery in utility investment and the fact that copper, the mainstay of power distribution grids worldwide, still has considerable potential to carry energy better and reduce losses than aluminium. 

Copper tube, which accounts for an estimated 13% of global refined copper consumption, is the largest of the copper product markets.  The two main uses are in plumbing and heating systems and in air conditioners and refrigeration (ACR tube).  The steady proliferation of plumbing amenities in and around the home, particularly as many houses built today within the mature economies have more than one bathroom, are largely responsible for copper plumbing tube demand growth, however, this is being offset by substitution to plastic tubing where this is possible.  Elsewhere, improved living standards in the developing economies, leading to higher demand for air conditioners, continues to boost demand for ACR tube.  This is particularly the case in China and India where improved power supply will lead to a surge in the consumption of air conditioners over the coming years.  Meanwhile in the mature economies, the market is being driven by external factors such as environmental issues, regulatory concerns and social demands for comfort. 

Other copper and copper alloy products consumed by the construction sector include copper sheet and strip, rods, bars and sections plus brass products.  Copper sheet is used for roofing, eaves gutters, drain pipes for rainwater and lining for facades, while rods bars and sections, along with brass products, are used for building fixture and fittings.  In hospitals, brass doorknobs and push plates are widely used because it has been proven that they help to reduce cross contamination. 

Electrical and electronic products are copper’s second largest consuming sector, accounting for 34% of total copper demand.  Copper containing electrical and electronic products include telecommunication cable, power cable, transformer windings, semiconductors, connectors and motors for heavy appliances. 

Since the early 1990s copper telecommunication cable has been largely substituted by fibre optic cable in long distance networks.  However, copper telecom cable has remained the preferred link between the main network and consumers. In addition, the development of the internet and e-mail has further enhanced the role of copper in telecommunications in recent years.  The need for information to be carried more quickly along the telecommunication network has led to the introduction of asymmetrical digital subscriber line technology (ADSL).  The ADSL is a dedicated circuit between a home and the telephone company’s central office that uses normal copper telephone lines.  The addition of an ADSL chip to the existing copper network means that us

ers can download files around 15 times faster than an analogue dial-up connection. 

Dramatic gains in copper consumption to have occurred within the home and office because of a system known to the telecommunications industry as ‘structured wiring’.  The cable carrying voice, computer and television signals is connected to a central hub in the home.  Individual cables then run independently from here to high-quality connections in rooms throughout the house.  Cables connected to the hub consist of four pairs of twisted wires, capable of carrying more electronic signals with less interference and resistance than the older four-stranded telephone wires. Prior to 1930, copper and brass, having excellent pressure containing and anticorrosion characteristics, were the favoured materials to be used in brake tubing.  However, mass auto production in the 1940s led to the adoption of furnace-brazed steel tubing because it was much lower in cost.  Although this form of tubing is still widely used today, copper has re-gained some of its lost market share through the introduction of a copper-nickel alloy (90% copper/10% nickel) which is more resistant to corrosion from road mud and salt than steel piping. Copper’s final end-use category is consumer and general products.  Copper consumed in this sector accounts for 9% of total copper consumption. The production of the Euro coin and the US presidential dollar coin in recent years has helped to support demand for copper and copper alloy products. This mis-match can become so acute that it is not realistic to assume that the market could behave in this manner. To overcome this situation, a market-driven adjustment is introduced in concentrates/precipitates and SxEw production capability. 

This adjustment is defined as that which is required to maintain an orderly market balance and is split into two categories in order to distinguish disruption allowances from closures/reactivations on account of price/market-related conditions. 

The “disruption allowance” moving forward is assumed to be 5% of the production capability projection at the start of each year.

A positive adjustment could be met either by new projects, incremental expansions or extensions to the mine-life of existing operations where closure is anticipated within the forecast period due to reserve depletions. These adjustments are made on an iterative basis, and are driven by the consumption forecast. These forecasts take into account the likely level of metal prices required to affect them, as well as the impact of changes in metal stocks on metal prices. Thus, during periods of surplus supplies, metal prices need to fall to a level sufficiently low to effect the closure of marginal mine capacity.
